opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really interesting question, because it points at something we still don't fully understand.

With some things humans are good at, like vision, locomotion, or a sense of danger, you can tell an evolutionary story. Our ancestors needed those abilities for hundreds of millions of years, so it's plausible that evolution gave us a very strong prior. Some of that learning was done in advance, so to speak.

Language, math, and coding are different. Language is fairly recent in evolutionary terms. Math and coding are extremely recent. There's no way evolution specifically prepared us for writing Python. And yet people learn these things remarkably well. A teenager can learn to drive in maybe ten hours of practice. Someone can become a competent programmer in a year or two, with a tiny fraction of the data our models see. And they come out more robust: they generalize better, and they don't make the strange mistakes models make.

So what does that suggest? It suggests humans aren't good at learning only because of domain-specific priors. There's something more general going on. Some underlying machinery for learning is simply better: more sample-efficient, better at generalization. That's a big deal, because if it were all priors, you'd say evolution did something special. But for math and coding, it's probably the learning algorithm itself.

I think one piece of it is that people have a very good internal sense of how they're doing. When you're learning to code or doing a proof, you don't need someone to grade every step. You have a feeling that this approach is going nowhere, or that this is elegant and right. That's something like a value function, and it's very robust in humans. It lets you learn continually, from your own experience, without an external reward for everything.

Another piece is the kind of learning itself. People don't memorize; they understand. Compare a student who does ten thousand competition problems and memorizes every trick with a student who practices for a hundred hours but has some real feel for the subject. The second one often does better in their career. Our models today are much more like the first student. They've been drilled on an enormous amount, and that's why they look brilliant on evals but generalize less well than you'd expect.

So I think the lesson from language, math, and coding is that there's a principle of learning that humans have and that we don't yet fully have in our machines. That's an existence proof that it's possible. I have opinions about what it might be, but I think it's one of the most important open questions in the field.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that math and coding learning cannot be explained by domain-specific priors alone and points to a more general learning machinery, likely the learning algorithm itself.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the striking thing is how different the three cases are, and yet they share something.

Take language. A child learns language from an amount of data that is, by machine learning standards, tiny. A few tens of millions of words by age five, maybe. And they don't get labeled data, they don't get gradients, they just hear people talk and somehow end up with a very robust competence. Nobody has to be good at language. Everyone gets it. That tells you the thing being learned is deeply matched to the learner. Whatever prior humans have, language fits it very well.

Math and coding are the opposite case. Here people vary enormously. Some people learn these things easily, most people find them hard, and almost nobody learns them without a lot of deliberate effort. So these are domains where the human prior is not doing the heavy lifting. What is doing the lifting?

If you look at the people who are good at math or coding, I don't think the distinguishing feature is that they memorize more. It's that they have a very good sense of when they don't understand something. They notice the small discomfort, the little feeling of "wait, that doesn't quite follow," and they stop and resolve it instead of moving on. A weaker learner will accept something that sort of makes sense. A strong learner refuses to. They want the thing to be fully coherent, and they keep pushing until it is. That's a kind of internal signal that is far richer than any external reward. And then they practice. They do many problems, they write a lot of code, they get things wrong and correct them. So the learning is self-directed in a very precise way, driven by this internal sense of what still needs work.

So what does that suggest about good learning in general? I would say three things. One, a good prior matters, and the clearest example of that is language. Two, the learner needs a reliable internal signal of understanding versus not understanding, because that is what makes small amounts of experience go a long way. And three, the learner has to act on that signal, has to go seek the experience that will fix the gap. Humans who are good at math and coding do that almost compulsively.

And I think this is relevant to the current moment in AI. Our systems are extraordinarily good at the first part, absorbing a huge amount of data, far more than any human. But they are much weaker at the second and third. They don't have a strong sense of what they don't understand, and they don't go and fix it. Humans are very sample efficient and the models are not, and I think the reason is mostly this. So when I think about what makes people good at learning, that is the part I find most interesting, because it is the part we have not yet figured out how to build.

r001.rationale: The response says the human prior does not do the heavy lifting in math and coding, then identifies learners’ internal sense of what they do not understand and their effort to resolve it as key to learning. This communicates a more fundamental basis than a complicated prior.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting thing is how little experience people need to learn some things, and how much they need to learn others. A child learns language without anyone explaining the rules. But with mathematics, you can spend a long time understanding one idea, and then suddenly it makes many other things easier to understand.

So being good at learning is not just about remembering more examples. It’s also about having the right prior knowledge, which lets you make sense of the next example. In coding, once you understand a few underlying concepts, you can encounter a new problem and recognize something familiar in it, even if it looks quite different.

But there is a question here: how much of that ability comes from learning, and how much comes from the structure we start with? Human learning gives us evidence that very efficient learning is possible. It doesn’t, by itself, tell us how to reproduce it.

r001.rationale: The response says prior knowledge and starting structure help learning, but it does not suggest that math and coding point to a basis more fundamental than a complicated prior.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one striking thing is how much people differ in the amount of experience they need. Two people can attend the same class, read the same book, do the same exercises, and come away with quite different levels of understanding. So clearly, the amount of data is not the whole explanation. Something about what the learner brings to the data matters a great deal.

And it’s not just memory. You can remember a mathematical statement without understanding why it’s true, or read a lot of code without becoming good at programming. The interesting step is finding the underlying structure, so that the next problem becomes easier because you understood the previous one.

But there’s a complication: we don’t really know how much prior experience is relevant. Someone may appear to learn something very quickly because they already have useful concepts from somewhere else. So I think human learning points toward the importance of good prior structure and the ability to reuse what you’ve learned. It doesn’t, by itself, tell us exactly how those abilities work.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes useful prior structure and reusing learned concepts, but does not suggest that learning ability has a basis more fundamental than a complicated prior.
